assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Frequency
items.clue: The number of waves passing a point each second.

items.label: Visible light
items.clue: The only group of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect.

items.label: Wavelength
items.clue: The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an electromagnetic wave?

options.text: A transverse wave that transfers energy from source to absorber
A longitudinal wave that transfers energy to an absorber
A transverse wave that transfers matter to an absorber
A transverse wave that needs air to carry its energy

questions.explanation: The specification defines electromagnetic waves as transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber.

questions.stem: A student is drawing a ray diagram for light passing from air into a glass block. Where should the angle of incidence be measured?

options.text: Between the incoming ray and the flat surface of the glass block itself.
Between the incoming ray and the refracted ray inside the block.
Between the incoming ray and the normal drawn at the point it enters.
Between the refracted ray and the flat surface of the block.

questions.explanation: The normal is the dashed line at right angles to the boundary at the point of entry, and both angles are measured from it.

options.text: In changes to the electrons of an atom
In bonds being broken between two atoms
In the heating of very dense material
In changes in the nucleus of an atom

questions.explanation: The specification states that gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

questions.stem: The specification lists a practical application for each group of electromagnetic waves. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Satellite communication uses radio waves
Sun tanning lamps mainly give out infrared
Fibre optic communications use visible light
A toaster cooks bread using microwaves

questions.explanation: The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications: the signal travels along the glass fibre as rapid pulses of light.

questions.stem: A transmitter sends radio waves to a distant aerial. What is transferred, and in which direction?

options.text: Particles of matter, from the transmitter to the aerial
Energy, from the source of the wave to the absorber
Energy, carried along by the air between them
Sound, from the transmitter to the radio aerial

questions.explanation: The wave transfers energy from the source (the transmitter) to the absorber (the aerial).

questions.stem: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0°. What should the ray diagram show?

options.text: The ray bends towards the normal as it enters, then bends back as it leaves.
The ray bends away from the normal as soon as it crosses into the glass.
The ray bends sideways as soon as it enters the glass block.
The ray carries straight on through the block without changing course.

questions.explanation: Along the normal every part of the wave front crosses the boundary at the same instant, so the wave slows but is not deviated.

questions.stem: Which statement about how electromagnetic waves are generated and absorbed is correct?

options.text: Only changes in the nuclei of atoms can generate these waves
Changes in atoms and in their nuclei generate and absorb them
Only changes in the electrons of an atom can generate them
Atoms generate these waves but can never absorb any of them

questions.explanation: The specification states that changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range.

questions.stem: Which use does the specification give for radio waves?

options.text: Broadcasting television and radio programmes
Sending signals to and from satellites in orbit
Carrying signals along fibre optic cables
Taking images of bones inside the body

questions.explanation: The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio.

questions.stem: How do the speeds of radio waves, visible light and gamma rays compare in a vacuum?

options.text: Gamma rays are fastest because they carry the most energy
Radio waves are slowest because their wavelength is longest
All of them travel at the same velocity in a vacuum
Visible light is faster than the radio waves are

questions.explanation: All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.

questions.stem: In Required practical activity 10 a Leslie cube is filled with hot water. An infrared detector is placed the same distance from each vertical face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?

options.text: All four read the same, because the water behind each face is at one temperature.
The shiny silver face, because polished metal gives out infrared best.
The matt white face, because pale surfaces give out the most radiation.
The matt black face, because matt black is the best emitter of infrared.

questions.explanation: A good absorber is also a good emitter, so the matt black face radiates most strongly at that temperature.

questions.stem: A worker's radiation dose is recorded in sieverts (Sv). What does this dose measure?

options.text: The number of nuclei decaying near the worker
The amount of radioactive material in the body
The risk of harm that results from the exposure
The frequency of the radiation entering the body

questions.explanation: The specification states that radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.

questions.stem: A signal is sent from a ground station up to a satellite in orbit and then back down to a second ground station. Which waves carry the signal?

options.text: Radio waves, which are used for broadcasting today
Microwaves, which pass through the atmosphere
Infrared, which is given out by all hot objects
Visible light, which goes in straight lines

questions.explanation: The specification pairs microwaves with satellite communications; the atmosphere transmits them, so they reach the satellite and return.

questions.stem: A hammer strikes one end of a long steel rail. A student with an ear pressed against the far end hears the blow. What is happening inside the steel as the sound travels along it?

options.text: Particles of the steel vibrate about their positions and pass the disturbance on
Sound slips along the tiny gaps of air trapped between the steel particles
Sound leaves the rail at once and reaches the ear through the air
The rail as a whole slides towards the listener as the wave passes

questions.explanation: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid: each particle vibrates and hands the disturbance to its neighbour.

questions.stem: A survey team sends waves down into the ground to look for a buried rock layer in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens when the waves reach the top of that buried layer?

options.text: The waves carry on downwards at exactly the same speed
Part of each wave is reflected back and the rest travels on
All of each wave is reflected and none of it travels on
The waves are all absorbed at the top of the buried layer

questions.stem: A sheet of window glass lets almost all of the visible light reaching it pass through, but it absorbs most of the ultraviolet. What does this show?

options.text: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
A material that looks clear to the eye must be transmitting every wave reaching it.
Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.
Any wave the glass does not transmit must be completely absorbed by it.

questions.stem: (HT only) How can radio waves be produced?

options.text: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
By heating a metal aerial till it glows
By changes in the nucleus of the atom
By changes in the electrons of an atom

questions.explanation: The specification states that radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

questions.stem: (HT only) Explain why microwaves rather than infrared are used to send signals to a communications satellite.

options.text: Microwaves travel much faster through space than infrared can
Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, infrared does not
Infrared cannot cross the vacuum of space, but microwaves do
Microwaves are the only waves a dish aerial can send

questions.explanation: The atmosphere transmits microwaves, so the signal reaches the satellite and returns; infrared is strongly absorbed by gases and water vapour in the air.

questions.stem: Music from a loudspeaker in one room can be heard through a solid brick wall in the room next door. Which statement best describes the part the wall plays?

options.text: It blocks the sound entirely, so what is heard has leaked round the edges
The brick itself vibrates and carries the sound wave to the far side
Sound seeps through the pores of trapped air inside the brick
It reflects the whole wave, so only an echo is heard nearby

questions.explanation: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid; the vibrating brick then radiates sound into the second room.
